lesson.title: Unequal Sharing: How Polarity Enters a Covalent Bond
lesson.summary: When two bonded atoms have different electronegativities, they do not share their bonding electron pair equally, and that unequal pull creates a small separation of charge called a bond dipole.
lesson.body:
A covalent bond is usually described as a shared pair of electrons, and that description is accurate, but it hides an important detail: shared does not automatically mean shared equally. Whether the electron pair sits exactly halfway between two nuclei, or is pulled noticeably closer to one of them, depends entirely on how strongly each atom attracts electrons, a property already introduced as electronegativity. Bond polarity is simply the name for what happens when that pull is unequal.

When one atom in a covalent bond is more electronegative than the other, it pulls the shared electron density toward itself. The electron cloud of the bond shifts, spending more time near the more electronegative atom than near the other. This does not transfer the electrons completely, the way an ionic bond would, but it does create a small, partial separation of charge: the more electronegative atom picks up a partial negative charge, written as delta minus, while the less electronegative atom is left with a partial positive charge, written as delta plus. These are fractional charges, far smaller than the full plus one or minus one charges found in ionic compounds, but they are real and they have real chemical consequences. The size of this charge separation is not fixed either. It scales with how large the electronegativity gap between the two bonded atoms is: a bond between two atoms with only a small gap carries just a slight partial charge, while a bond between two atoms with a large gap, such as hydrogen and fluorine, carries a much larger partial charge, though still short of a full unit charge.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is a standard worked example. Chlorine is considerably more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electron pair in the H-Cl bond spends more time around the chlorine atom. This gives chlorine a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge, written as H delta plus, Cl delta minus. This lopsided distribution of electron density across the bond is what chemists mean by a bond dipole.

By contrast, when the two bonded atoms have identical or nearly identical electronegativities, neither one wins the tug of war, and the electron pair remains essentially centered between them. The clearest cases are bonds between two atoms of the same element, such as the H-H bond in H2 or the Cl-Cl bond in Cl2, where the two atoms are, by definition, equally electronegative and share the bonding pair exactly equally. These are called nonpolar covalent bonds, and they sit at the opposite end of the spectrum from a strongly polar bond.

Bond polarity is best thought of as a continuum rather than a strict either or category, running from perfectly equal sharing at one end to essentially complete electron transfer at the other. Where any particular bond falls on that continuum depends on exactly how large the electronegativity gap between its two atoms is. Turning that idea into a concrete, comparable number for any pair of atoms is exactly the job of electronegativity difference, covered next.
